prize_parts.citation: for the development of targeted protein degradation using bifunctional degraders and molecular glues

statement.case_for: Targeted protein degradation meets my standard of a game-changer: a simple chemical idea, a bifunctional molecule that brings a target protein to an E3 ligase, that created a genuinely new drug modality with event-driven, catalytic pharmacology. The mechanism is quantitatively understood (ternary-complex cooperativity, turnover), has been confirmed independently in many laboratories, and has already led to a large clinical pipeline. Crews and Deshaies provided the original PROTAC concept and proof of principle. After reading Daniel Aili's opening I now put Handa rather than Ciulli in the third seat: identifying cereblon as the thalidomide target gives the molecular-glue strand a clear mechanistic origin that explains an old drug and underlies the CRBN-recruiting degraders, and it keeps both strands under a single citation.
statement.case_against: No degrader is yet a broadly established approved therapy, so the translational case is still partly prospective. The three-person limit also forces an uncomfortable choice among Ciulli (VHL ligands, structural basis), Gray, Sakamoto, Ito and Kim, and the PROTAC and glue strands arose somewhat independently, so a single citation could be criticised as merging two discoveries. If the committee judges the clinical evidence premature, B048 or B017 are mature or clearly impactful alternatives.

responses.point: Aili supports Crews, Deshaies and Handa, arguing that Handa's cereblon work underpins the molecular-glue branch and that these three form the most defensible core, while admitting that Ciulli, Gray and Sakamoto complicate attribution.
responses.response: I find this persuasive and have moved from Ciulli to Handa. Ciulli's VHL ligands made PROTACs more drug-like, which is an important optimisation. Handa's identification of cereblon is a separate mechanistic discovery that changed how a whole drug class is understood. I share Aili's reservation about chronology and clinical maturity, and I would want the committee to confirm that the early PROTAC reports have clear priority before settling the third name.

responses.point: Sparr ranks phase separation first, as a new thermodynamic description of cellular organisation with Hyman, Brangwynne and Rosen as the core, while acknowledging that physiological relevance in vivo is still debated.
responses.response: I respect the physical-chemical framing, and phase separation is certainly a new organising principle. But the in vivo debate is exactly the issue: it is not yet clear which condensates are truly liquid and functionally phase-separated, and the work has produced less demonstrated consequence than degraders. It also sits uneasily on the boundary with the physiology or medicine prize. I would hold it back for later, not place it in this year's configuration.

responses.point: Somfai ranks Pd-catalysed C-N coupling first as a mature, widely used method with Buchwald and Hartwig as the core, noting that the 2010 cross-coupling prize may make some hesitant.
responses.response: I agree this is a clear case of simple, general chemistry adopted everywhere, and the maturity argument is strong. My reservation is the closeness to the 2010 prize: C-N coupling is an important extension rather than a new principle, and the committee has to decide whether it is a distinct achievement. That is a fair question, but I do not think it outweighs the novelty of degradation, which is why I rank it below B056. I could see it as a second part if the committee prefers a mature synthetic achievement.

responses.point: Brzezinski ranks nitrogenase first, as a physical-chemical problem of the first rank where structure and mechanism of the FeMo-cofactor were established through crystallography and kinetics, with Rees, Einsle and Seefeldt as the core.
responses.response: Peter and I have served together since 2015, and I take his scientific argument seriously: the interstitial carbide and the ATP-gated electron delivery are remarkable. My concern is the attribution among Rees, Einsle, Seefeldt, Dean and Ribbe, and the catalytic cycle is still not settled. As a simulation person I would want the mechanism understood quantitatively before rewarding it as a completed achievement, so I would not put it ahead of degradation, though it is a credible later candidate.

responses.point: Linke ranks degraders first with Crews, Deshaies and Ciulli, stressing the event-driven catalytic principle, and treats base editing as a strong case for Liu alone, with some concern about proximity to the 2020 CRISPR prize.
responses.response: I agree on the degradation principle and the quantitative picture. On base editing I side with Linke that Liu alone is the more defensible attribution, since Nishida and Kondo's parallel work blurs the position of the trainees, and I would give the proximity to the CRISPR prize real weight. This is why I list B048 only as an alternative, and why a Liu-only citation there is a better fallback than a three-name one.

uncertainties: Whether the third seat for B056 should go to Handa (cereblon and molecular glues) or Ciulli (VHL ligands and structural basis), and whether a single citation can cover both PROTAC and glue strands.
Whether the clinical evidence for degraders is sufficient or whether an approved drug is needed first.
Whether base editing (B048) should be attributed to Liu alone given the Nishida and Kondo parallel work.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for the shortlisted ballots. My Warshel and EVB connections and my work in computational biochemistry are not tied to any shortlisted candidate. I have served with Peter Brzezinski since 2015, but that is a committee relationship, not a conflict.
